Sequential AIPE Check for a Contrast

Source: R/seq_aipe_c.R
seq_aipe_c.Rd

Checks, with the data collected so far from K independent groups, whether enough observations are in hand for a confidence interval for a contrast of the group means, \(\psi = \sum_{k=1}^{K} c_k \mu_k\) (for example one condition against the average of two others), that is no wider than a chosen width, without assuming normality or equal variances and without planning values. The contrast is one of the effect sizes covered by the sequential accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) procedure of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, Example 6).

Usage

seq_aipe_c(groups, contrast_weights, width, conf_level = 0.95)

Arguments

groups

A list of K numeric vectors (K at least 2), one per group: the observations collected so far from each population. Every vector needs at least 4 observations and all must have the same length; missing or infinite values are an error. A matrix or data frame is not accepted (a data frame in "long" format would be misread); with one column per group use as.list(as.data.frame(m)), and with an outcome y and a grouping variable g use split(y, g).

contrast_weights

A numeric vector of K contrast weights \(c_k\), in the order of groups (see "Names" in Details). They must be finite and not all zero.

width

The target full width of the confidence interval for the contrast (\(\omega\) in the cited article): the upper limit minus the lower limit, in the units of the outcome. A single positive number.

conf_level

The confidence level of the interval, a single number strictly between 0 and 1. Default 0.95.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") (see smsd_check_methods for its print(), summary(), and tidy() methods) with one row per quantity and columns term and value. The rows are, in order:

lower_limit

the lower confidence limit (NA when the variance estimate is not yet usable or the estimate cannot be computed; see the section below);

contrast

the estimated contrast;

upper_limit

the upper confidence limit (NA whenever lower_limit is);

xi_squared

the estimated asymptotic variance \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\), at least \(n^{-3}\) (the bound itself when the estimate is not yet usable);

criterion_n

the per group sample size the stopping rule currently requires (at least current_n + 1 when the variance estimate is not yet usable or the estimate cannot be computed);

current_n

the current per group sample size (the total sample size is K times this).

The object also carries these attributes:

is_satisfied

TRUE when the stopping rule is met, otherwise FALSE; never NA, and always identical to current_n >= criterion_n;

method

the string "contrast";

n_per_group

an integer vector with the size of each group, named when groups is;

contrast_weights

the weights, as doubles;

current_n, criterion_n

the values in the rows of those names (both per group);

conf_level, width

the values supplied;

variance_unusable

TRUE when the raw variance estimate is zero, negative, or not finite (see the section below), otherwise FALSE;

notes

a character vector, empty unless something needs explaining.

Details

The function evaluates the stopping rule once and returns. The user collects the pilot sample from every group (see seq_aipe_c_pilot), calls seq_aipe_c(), and, while the rule is not met, adds the same number of observations to every group and calls it again. The function prints nothing and keeps no state.

Estimate. The contrast is estimated by \(\hat{\psi}_n = \sum_k c_k \bar{X}_{kn}\), the weighted sum of the group means (their Equation 16). The article writes the weights as summing to one; the procedure does not depend on that, and any weights that are finite and not all zero are accepted (weights that sum to zero give a comparison among groups).

Stopping rule. With \(n\) observations in each group, sampling stops at the first \(n\), at or after the pilot size, with $$n \ge \left\lceil \frac{4 z_{\alpha/2}^2}{\omega^2} \left(\hat{\xi}_n^2 + \frac{1}{n}\right) \right\rceil$$ (their Equation 22), where \(\hat{\xi}_n^2 = \sum_k c_k^2 s_{kn}^2\) estimates the asymptotic variance of \(\sqrt{n}(\hat{\psi}_n - \psi)\). The reported interval is \(\hat{\psi}_n \pm z_{\alpha/2} \hat{\xi}_n / \sqrt{n}\) (their Equation 23). Whenever the rule is met, the width of that interval is at most width.

Balanced data. The function implements the balanced procedure of the article's Example 6, which adds an observation to every group at each stage, so every group must have the same number of observations. Groups of unequal size are an error rather than a fallback: a rule applied group by group cannot guarantee the requested width. Bring every group up to the common size and call the function again. The article also outlines an extension to unbalanced designs (its Equations 39 to 47), in which the optimal group sizes are proportional to \(c_k \sigma_k\) and are to be estimated sequentially; the article prints no stopping rule for it, and that extension is not implemented.

Units. Unlike a standardized effect size, the contrast and width are in the units of the outcome, while the correction term \(1/n\) in the stopping rule and the lower bound \(n^{-3}\) on the variance estimate are pure numbers, as printed in the article. They play their intended roles (a small correction, and a bound far below any plausible estimate) when \(\xi^2\) is not many orders of magnitude from one. If the outcome is recorded in units that make its variance very small or very large, rescale it (and width with it) first. When the variance estimate is positive but below \(n^{-3}\), which on ordinary scales a weighted sum of sample variances essentially never is, the bound is used in its place, as the article prescribes, so the interval is wider and the required sample size larger than the estimate itself would give; a note on the returned object says that this happened and advises rescaling.

A group with no variation. When every observation in a group with a nonzero weight is the same (values that agree to ten significant digits count as the same), the variance of that group has not been estimated, and so neither has the variance of the contrast: the contrast is still estimated, but the check reports the rule as not met and a note names the group (see the section below), as seq_budget does with the same data. Summing the variances of the other groups instead would leave the constant group out of the variance of the contrast. In simulated studies of three groups answering a 5 point item, one of them with 70% of its answers at the top of the scale (weights 1, -1/2, -1/2, width = 2, 4,000 studies), 23% of the studies would have stopped with that group constant, after 4 to 7 observations per group, and 74% of their intervals covered the contrast; with the group treated as not yet estimated, coverage over all studies was 0.934 against 0.899. The price is paid where a group stays constant: for binary outcomes with proportions 0.30, 0.02, and 0.02 (width = 0.5, 2,000 studies) the mean final sample size was 75 per group against 18, and coverage 0.939 against 0.891. If a group shows no variation well past the pilot sample, reconsider the measure. A group whose weight is zero takes no part in the contrast and is not looked at.

Names. groups and contrast_weights are matched by position. If both are named, the names must be the same and in the same order; otherwise the function stops, so that weights named in another order (for example against a list made by split(), which is in alphabetical order) are not applied to the wrong groups.

What the guarantee is. The width guarantee is exact. The coverage guarantee is asymptotic: coverage approaches conf_level as width shrinks (their Theorem 2). In simulated studies with a 95% interval and one observation per group added at each stage, coverage for three normal groups with unit variances and weights 1, -1/2, -1/2 was 0.948 at width = 0.4 (6,000 studies, about 144 per group at the end) and 0.945 at width = 0.2 (2,000 studies, about 577 per group); for three groups with skewed distributions and unequal variances it was 0.949 and 0.951 (Monte Carlo standard errors 0.003 and 0.005). At a wide target the final sample is small and coverage falls a little short: with means 0.5, 0, and 0 it was 0.936 at width = 1 (10,000 studies, about 23 per group). The variance estimate, a weighted sum of sample variances, cannot be negative, and it was never below its lower bound in these studies.

Estimates That Are Not Yet Usable

When the raw variance estimate is zero (exactly, or to within rounding error), negative, or not finite, which is common at small sample sizes for some effect sizes, or when the point estimate cannot be computed (a sample with no variation, where values that agree to ten significant digits count as equal), the check reports the stopping rule as not met, sets attr(out, "variance_unusable") to TRUE, and attaches a note that print() shows; see smsd_check_methods. This is a deliberate departure from the stopping rule as printed in the source articles, under which the lower bound \(n^{-3}\) would stand in for such an estimate and the rule would be met at once with an interval far narrower than requested; a positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe (the larger of it and \(n^{-3}\)).

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Maxwell, S. E., Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2008). Sample size planning for statistical power and accuracy in parameter estimation. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 537–563. doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093735

See also

seq_aipe_c_pilot for the pilot size, and seq_budget for a sequential interval for a contrast when the groups have different sampling costs and there is a budget. In DMAR: ss_aipe_c, the fixed sample size analog for when planning values are available, ss_aipe_sc for the standardized contrast, and ci_c.

Other seq_aipe_c: seq_aipe_c_pilot(), seq_aipe_sensitivity

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Francis Bilson Darku fbilsond@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Does a new onboarding program change first year performance ratings
# (standardized) relative to the average of two existing programs? The
# aim is a 95% confidence interval for that contrast no wider than 0.80.
set.seed(113)
program_means <- c(new = 0.5, existing_a = 0, existing_b = 0)
weights <- c(1, -0.5, -0.5)
m <- seq_aipe_c_pilot(width = 0.80)
ratings <- lapply(program_means, function(mu) rnorm(m, mean = mu))
out <- seq_aipe_c(ratings, weights, width = 0.80)
out
#> Sequential check (contrast)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 5
#>   Criterion n     : 42
#>   Target width    : 0.8
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -0.3410512
#>   contrast          : 0.7461581
#>   upper_limit       : 1.833367
#>   xi_squared        : 1.538509
#>   criterion_n       : 42
#>   current_n         : 5
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# The rule is not met at the pilot. Add one employee to every program and
# check again, until it is.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  ratings <- Map(function(r, mu) c(r, rnorm(1, mean = mu)),
                 ratings, program_means)
  out <- seq_aipe_c(ratings, weights, width = 0.80)
}
out
#> Sequential check (contrast)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 44
#>   Criterion n     : 44
#>   Target width    : 0.8
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -0.0953664
#>   contrast          : 0.2997286
#>   upper_limit       : 0.6948236
#>   xi_squared        : 1.787967
#>   criterion_n       : 44
#>   current_n         : 44
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
attr(out, "n_per_group")
#>        new existing_a existing_b 
#>         44         44         44
